title: Nuclear Power
objective: After this level you can explain how splitting atoms heats water in a nuclear power plant.
summary: Neutrons split uranium-235 in a controlled chain reaction; the heat makes steam for a turbine, with no CO2 while running. Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years.

cards.headline: One uranium pellet holds about as much energy as a ton of coal.
cards.body: That's the US Department of Energy's comparison, for one small ceramic pellet. The energy comes from splitting atoms. And here's the surprise: once that energy is out, a nuclear plant uses it the same way Level 12's coal plant does.

cards.headline: Splitting atoms, on purpose
cards.body: Nuclear plants use uranium-235, whose atoms split easily. A neutron strikes a uranium atom and splits it, releasing a lot of energy as heat and radiation, plus more neutrons. Those neutrons split more atoms: a chain reaction. Reactors keep it under control with control rods, pushed in to slow the reaction and pulled out to speed it up. A fire made of atoms, with a dimmer switch.

cards.headline: Then it's a kettle again
cards.body: The uranium, made into pellets and sealed in metal fuel rods, heats water into steam. The steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator, just like in a coal plant. The difference is what's missing: nuclear reactors release no carbon dioxide or air pollution while they run. In 2025 they made about 18% of US electricity and about 9% of the world's.

cards.headline: Why people argue about it
cards.body: Spent fuel is highly radioactive and can stay dangerous for thousands of years. The US still has no permanent place to put it, so it waits in pools of water and dry containers. Views split sharply. The International Energy Agency says nuclear power can play a major role in cutting emissions. Greenpeace opposes new plants, calling nuclear power dangerous and expensive and pointing to waste and to the Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents.

questions.prompt: In a nuclear reactor, the chain reaction is kept going by _____.

options.label: steam pressing on the uranium
options.rationale: Steam is made by the heat; it doesn't split atoms.

options.label: the plant's own electricity
options.rationale: The reaction makes the heat; it isn't powered by electricity.

questions.explanation: Each split releases more neutrons, which split more uranium-235 atoms. Control rods slow it down.

questions.prompt: Match each part of nuclear power with its description.

pairs.right: Pushed in to slow the reaction

questions.explanation: Uranium-235's atoms split easily, control rods are pushed in to slow the reaction, and spent fuel is highly radioactive.

questions.prompt: What does a nuclear plant have in common with a coal plant?

options.label: Both burn fuel in a boiler
options.rationale: A reactor splits atoms; nothing burns.

options.label: Both release carbon dioxide while running
Both heat water into steam that spins a turbine
Both use control rods
options.rationale: Control rods are only in nuclear reactors.

questions.explanation: Split atoms or burning coal, the heat boils water, and steam spins the turbine and generator.
